title: Mangrove

definition.text: A mangrove is a tree or shrub that lives mostly in salty or brackish coastal water; the word also names the coastal vegetation these plants form.

facts.text: Mangroves grow along tropical and subtropical coasts, mostly between 30° N and 30° S, with the largest area within 5° of the equator.
Special adaptations let them take in extra oxygen and get rid of salt, so they survive where most plants die.
In 2025 the world's mangroves were estimated to cover 15.9 million hectares, with Asia holding the largest share at 6.10 million ha.
Indonesia, Brazil, Australia, Nigeria and Mexico together hold almost half (49%) of global mangrove area.
Human activity keeps destroying mangroves at an estimated 0.16% a year worldwide, and up to 0.70% a year in some countries.
A 2022 study estimated a net loss of 3,700 km2 of mangroves worldwide between 1999 and 2019.
Mangroves support coastal and marine ecosystems, shield nearby land from tsunamis and extreme weather, and store carbon well.
Although a mangrove forest has few tree species, it gives habitat to many other species, including up to 174 species of marine megafauna.

title: Mangrove adaptations to salt and flooding

definition.text: Mangroves have evolved special roots, leaves and seeds that let them cope with salty water, waterlogged mud and tides.

facts.text: Some mangroves grow pneumatophores, root-like tubes that stick up out of the mud like straws so the plant can breathe.
Red mangrove roots are coated with suberin and act as a filter that keeps most sodium salts out of the plant.
Many mangroves are viviparous: their seeds sprout while still on the parent tree, then drop as floating seedlings that water can carry far away.
Different mangrove species tolerate water from brackish, through seawater at 3 to 4% salinity, up to 9% salinity.

title: Mangroves as coastal protection

definition.text: Mangrove swamps act as a natural barrier that protects coasts from erosion, storm surges and tsunamis.

facts.text: Their huge root systems absorb wave energy, limiting erosion from high-energy waves during storm surges and tsunamis.
By slowing incoming tides, mangroves make sediment settle out, so they build up the land they grow on.
Studies show mangroves give coastal communities measurable economic protection against tropical storms.
Because of this erosion protection, mangroves are often targeted by conservation programmes, including national biodiversity action plans.
Removing mangroves disturbs the sediments beneath them, which trap heavy metals, and can release that contamination into seawater.
Wave energy may fall by 75 per cent as a wave passes through 200 meters of mangrove forest.
Shorelines covered by mangroves erode less, or much more slowly, than bare shorelines when waves are strong.
Keeping a healthy mangrove forest is cheaper than seawalls, which can increase erosion in front of the wall and on neighbouring land.

distinct_from: Mangrove adaptations to salt and flooding

title: Mangroves as fish nurseries

definition.text: The tangle of mangrove roots forms a sheltered underwater habitat where young fish and other sea animals grow up.

facts.text: Submerged roots carry algae, barnacles, oysters and sponges, while shrimps and mud lobsters live in the muddy bottom.
Lemon sharks give birth in mangrove creeks, where pups find cover and practise hunting with few predators.
Mangroves in Vietnam, Thailand, the Philippines and India support several commercially important fish and crustacean species.

distinct_from: Mangrove adaptations to salt and flooding

title: Mangrove carbon storage

definition.text: Mangrove forests take up carbon and lock it away in their wood and sediments, making them an important store of coastal 'blue carbon'.

facts.text: Mangrove forests are among the most carbon-rich biomes and account for 11% of the carbon that flows from land into the oceans.
Mangroves worldwide stored 4.19 Gt of carbon in 2012.
Two percent of mangrove carbon was lost between 2000 and 2012, equal to at most 0.316996250 Gt of carbon dioxide emissions.
Fallen mangrove material can turn into peat; termites help by processing litter and wood into their nests, which get buried.

definition.text: Forest ecology is the scientific study of the living things, patterns and processes found in forest ecosystems.

facts.text: A forest ecosystem is all the plants, animals and microbes of a woodland working together with its non-living physical surroundings.
Forest ecology usually studies whole populations, communities or ecosystems rather than single organisms.
Because trees vary so much in size and arrangement, forests are patchy, varied environments, and this variety supports great biodiversity.
Forests cover almost a third of all land, so forest ecology affects the whole biosphere and the human activities it supports.
Managing forests is called forestry, silviculture or forest management.
Machine learning now lets forest ecologists process larger and more complex data sets.

definition.text: Forests provide many benefits to the planet and to people, from oxygen and carbon storage to water regulation, soil protection, habitat and products.

facts.text: Forests produce about 28% of Earth's oxygen and act as crucial carbon sinks.
They host 80% of all land-dwelling organisms.
People rely directly on forests for fuel and wood products; the boreal forest alone supplies much lumber and paper.
Trees store large amounts of water and help regulate groundwater, evaporation and rain and snow patterns.
Without forests, erosion and sediment production get worse; removing or compacting leaf litter worsens erosion and flooding.
About 399 million ha of forest are set aside mainly to protect soil and water, 119 million ha more than in 1990.
Forests help drive the water cycle through a 'biotic pump' that draws moisture in from the ocean.

definition.text: Forests are threatened mainly by clearing for timber, land, mining, cities and farming, and by climate change.

facts.text: Deforestation removes large areas of forest for timber and land development.
Clearing breaks forest into smaller patches, making it harder for forest species to find food, shelter and mates, which cuts biodiversity.
Mining clears native forest and its logging and smelting cause soil erosion and acidification that slow recovery.
Farming turns forest into farmland and monocultures and brings in fertilizers and pesticides that harm the soil.
Urbanization splits habitats with roads, cities and infrastructure, displacing wildlife.
Climate change harms forests through wildfires, droughts, soil erosion and heat stress.

definition.text: A mycorrhizal network is a partnership in which fungi and plants share resources through connections in the soil.

facts.text: Fungal threads reach farther into the soil than roots, helping plants get phosphorus and water.
The network can move water and nutrients between plants and can help them resist drought.
Many conifers trade sugars to the fungi for nutrients, and some cannot survive without them.
The benefit varies by plant species and shrinks where soil nutrients are plentiful.

definition.text: Forests build up large amounts of living plant material, or biomass, and many do so quickly, making them highly productive.

facts.text: The world's forests hold about 606 gigatonnes of living biomass above and below ground plus 59 gigatonnes of dead wood.
This stored biomass can be released suddenly by fires and treefalls, which reshape forest structure.

definition.text: Coarse woody debris is dead wood such as fallen trunks and branches, which decays slowly on the forest floor.

facts.text: Wood rots slowly compared with most organic matter because of its chemistry, especially lignin, and decays even more slowly in dry or cold places.
Lying for long periods, it shapes wildlife habitat, fire behaviour and how trees regenerate.

definition.text: A kelp forest is an underwater area densely grown with kelp, a large brown seaweed; smaller patches are called kelp beds.

facts.text: Kelp forests are counted among the most productive and dynamic ecosystems on Earth.
Together with coral reefs they cover only 0.1% of Earth's surface yet account for 0.9% of global primary productivity.
They grow along temperate and polar coasts worldwide, and in 2007 were also found in tropical waters near Ecuador.
Kelp acts as an ecosystem engineer, providing the physical habitat for fish, invertebrates, seals, sea otters and seabirds.
Kelp forests can shape coastal ocean patterns and provide many ecosystem services.
Overfishing and climate change have all but wiped out kelp forests in vulnerable places such as Tasmania's east coast and Northern California.

definition.text: A kelp forest is built in layers, from tall canopy kelps reaching the surface down to kelps and algae on the sea floor, and this structure decides which species live there.

facts.text: Canopy kelps such as giant kelp form floating canopies at the ocean surface.
Stipitate kelps stand a few meters above the sea floor, and prostrate kelps lie along it; together they form the understory.
Beneath them lies a bottom layer of other algae and attached animals.

definition.text: In a kelp forest trophic cascade, the loss of predators such as sea otters lets sea urchins multiply and graze away the kelp.

facts.text: In Alaska, sea otters are the keystone species that keeps herbivorous urchins in check by eating them.
When otters are removed, for instance by hunting, urchin numbers soar, kelp is overgrazed and the species that depend on it are lost.
In Southern California several predators, including lobsters and large fish, control urchins, so losing one predator matters less there than in Alaska.
The shift from kelp forest to urchin-dominated 'urchin barren' is widespread, and the two are seen as alternative stable states of the ecosystem.
Kelp can recover from a barren after big shocks such as urchin disease or large temperature shifts.
Bottom-up control works the other way: nutrient-rich upwelling lets kelp grow and feed herbivores and the animals that eat them.

definition.text: Kelp forests give people food, materials, recreation and other benefits, which are ecosystem services specific to these forests.

facts.text: Kelp forests have mattered to people for thousands of years.
Modern fisheries for kelp-associated species such as lobster and rockfish support local economies.
Kelp is harvested to feed farmed abalone and to extract alginic acid, used in toothpaste and antacids.
Recreation such as scuba diving and kayaking brings both industry income and personal enjoyment, two separate benefits of the ecosystem.
One theory holds that the first people to reach the Americas followed a 'kelp highway' of Pacific kelp forests during the last ice age.

definition.text: Kelp takes up carbon as it grows, and when it sinks to the deep ocean floor that carbon can stay stored away from human disturbance.

facts.text: Macroalgae such as kelp take up 200 million tons of carbon dioxide every year.
Kelp forests around Australia were estimated to store 1.3-2.8 teragrams of carbon per year, 27–34% of the continent's annual coastal blue carbon.

verification.title: Substantial blue carbon in overlooked Australian kelp forests
verification.evidence: We reveal that these kelp forests represent 10.3–22.7 Tg C and contribute 1.3–2.8 Tg C year −1 in sequestered production, amounting to more than 30% of total blue carbon stored and sequestered around the Australian continent, and ~ 3% of the total global blue carbon.

definition.text: Kelp forests are threatened mainly by overfishing, pollution, kelp harvesting, invasive species and climate change.

facts.text: Overfishing may be the most pressing threat, because removing predators lets the forest collapse into an urchin barren.
The 2022 IPCC report says kelp and other seaweeds are suffering mass die-offs and range shifts from extreme heat in most regions.
In the 2010s Northern California lost 95% of its kelp ecosystems to marine heatwaves.
Pollution such as sewage, industrial chemicals, heavy metals and farm runoff has damaged kelp forests in southern California.
Managers often limit kelp harvesting and fishing, but this does not protect the whole ecosystem; marine protected areas cover the wider web of interactions.
Restoration in California mainly removes sea urchins, using divers and sea otters.

title: Salt marsh

definition.text: A salt marsh is a coastal wetland between land and sea that is regularly flooded by tides and covered with dense salt-tolerant herbs, grasses or low shrubs.

facts.text: Salt marshes form on sheltered, low-energy shores of temperate and high latitudes, such as estuaries and the back side of barrier islands.
In the tropics and subtropics they are replaced by mangroves, which are dominated by salt-tolerant trees instead of herbaceous plants.
Marsh plants trap and bind sediment, which keeps the marsh stable.
Salt marshes feed coastal food webs, deliver nutrients to coastal waters, support land animals and protect coasts.
They serve as sheltered feeding and nursery grounds for migratory fish.
Measured as net productivity, salt marshes are matched only by tropical rainforests.
A later study conservatively put global saltmarsh area at 90,800 km2, with the largest marshes outside the tropics.

title: Salt marsh formation

definition.text: A salt marsh forms when mudflats build up with sediment until tides flood them less often, letting plants take root.

facts.text: Rivers slow down as they reach the flat tidal zone and drop their sediment, helped by the rising tide.
Pioneer plants catch more sediment around their stems, forming mounds that join into raised terraces bound by roots.
As the surface rises, flooding gets shorter and shallower, and a succession of plant communities moves in.

distinct_from: Salt marshes and sea level rise

title: Human impacts on salt marshes

definition.text: Salt marshes have been heavily damaged by people, who long treated them as coastal wastelands to be drained, built on or polluted.

facts.text: They were lost to land reclamation for farming, urban development, salt production and recreation.
As of 2002, over half the world's population was estimated to live within 60 km of the coast, putting coastal habitats under heavy pressure.
A 2022 study blamed direct human activity for 22% of saltmarsh loss from 1999 to 2019, while 30% of gains came from deliberate actions such as restoration.
Urban development of marshes has slowed since about 1970 as people recognised the ecosystem services they provide.
Sea level rise driven by climate change also threatens marshes through erosion and drowning.

distinct_from: Salt marshes and sea level rise

title: Salt marsh land reclamation

definition.text: Land reclamation turned salt marsh into dry farmland, often by building dikes that kept the tide out.

facts.text: Reclamation changed vegetation, sediment, salinity and water flow, caused biodiversity loss and added nutrients.
Abandoned reclaimed land may stay barren for decades: in one English estuary little vegetation returned in 60–75 years because the ground was too low and compacted.

distinct_from: Salt marshes and sea level rise

title: Nitrogen loading in salt marshes
article: Salt marsh#Urban development and nitrogen loading

definition.text: Nitrogen loading is the extra nitrogen from sewage, urban runoff and farm and industrial waste that flows into salt marshes and changes their plant life.

facts.text: Salt marsh plants are normally limited by nitrogen, so extra nutrients reshuffle which species win the competition.
The aggressive reed Phragmites australis can invade disturbed marshes and crowd out native plants, harming insects and birds too.

distinct_from: Salt marshes and sea level rise

title: Salt marshes and sea level rise

definition.text: Rising seas threaten to flood and erode salt marshes, but marshes can sometimes build themselves up fast enough to keep pace.

facts.text: Rising water opens pools inside the marsh whose edges erode until the marsh can break up into open water.
Marsh plants slow currents and calm waves so that sediment settles, which helps the plants grow and trap still more: a positive bio-geomorphic feedback.
A marsh survives only if its surface rises faster than the sea; otherwise it drowns.
Mean sea level could rise between 0.6m to 1.1m by 2100.
Marshes also need accommodation space to move inland, which is often blocked by coastal roads, sea walls and other development.

title: Mosquito ditching of salt marshes

definition.text: In the early 20th century people dug straight ditches through salt marshes, believing that draining them would reduce mosquitoes.

facts.text: The ditches destroyed habitat for killifish, which eat mosquitoes, so mosquito numbers actually rose and wading birds lost food.
The ditches are still visible despite efforts to refill them.

distinct_from: Salt marshes and sea level rise

title: Salt marsh restoration

definition.text: Salt marsh restoration brings damaged or reclaimed marshes back toward their natural state, a practice that has grown since the 1980s.

facts.text: Once seen as wasteland, salt marshes are now recognised as among the most productive habitats on Earth, rivalling tropical rainforests.
Many countries now protect them by law; the US Clean Water Act and the EU Habitats Directive give them strong protection.
Restoration can use managed retreat or reclamation of land, either leaving a site to recover naturally or actively rebuilding the habitat.
Natural recovery can take 2–10 years or longer; replanting native vegetation speeds it up and usually works better.
Effective restoration takes considerable time and effort and needs careful long-term monitoring.
Fast-growing coastal populations in parts of Asia still tend to ignore marsh value and keep reclaiming the land.

distinct_from: Salt marshes and sea level rise

title: Salt marsh microbes
article: Salt marsh#Microbial life in salt marshes

definition.text: Microbes do most of the nutrient cycling and chemical processing in salt marshes, thriving in their salty, low-oxygen mud.

facts.text: Sulfate-reducing bacteria thrive in the oxygen-poor sediment and can account for up to 50% of the breakdown of organic matter there.
These bacteria help recycle nutrients and reduce nitrate pollution.
Cyanobacteria are important nitrogen fixers, supplying nitrogen to diatoms and microalgae.

distinct_from: Salt marshes and sea level rise

definition.text: An urban ecosystem is the ecosystem of a city, town or industrial area, a complex patchwork of buildings, roads, parks and gardens created and maintained by people.

facts.text: Urban ecosystems depend on large imports of water, nutrients, food and other resources.
Dense human populations interacting with many patch types produce complex feedbacks among the parts of the ecosystem.
Social-ecology treats cities as part of a wider social-ecological system linking urban communities with surrounding landscapes.
Cities hold more than half of the world's population, and urban numbers are expected to keep growing.
Cities offer jobs, healthcare and education, but urban growth worsens pollution and the loss of green space and biodiversity.
Studying urban ecosystems has led to proposals for sustainable urban design that reduces harm to surrounding environments.

definition.text: Urban ecology, including the study of the services that urban nature provides, is a young field whose research is still limited and unevenly spread.

facts.text: A review found a strong bias toward the northern hemisphere, with case studies mostly in the United States and China.
A review of 217 papers found most urban ecosystem service studies were done in Europe, North America and China at city scale.
Assessments use biophysical models, GIS and valuation, but few findings have been turned into land use policy.
Researchers are building better tools to map services such as water regulation, air cooling and water purification.

definition.text: Growing cities face pollution, loss of green space, habitat fragmentation, invasive species, urban heat and disease.

facts.text: Air pollution from vehicles, factories and power plants exceeds safe limits in many cities and causes respiratory and heart disease.
Forests, wetlands and grasslands are replaced by development, and losing green space lowers air and water quality, health and biodiversity.
Heavily urbanized areas have more invasive species than rural ones.
Urban heat islands make extreme heat more frequent, hitting the elderly and people without cooling hardest.

definition.text: Green and blue infrastructure means building in ways that weave natural systems such as vegetation and water into human-made structures.

facts.text: Green infrastructure includes nature preserves and added vegetation such as vertical gardens.
Blue infrastructure includes stormwater management such as bioswales.
LEED-certified buildings report using 30% less energy and gaining economic and mental benefits from natural light.

title: Wetland

definition.text: A wetland is a semi-aquatic ecosystem whose ground is flooded or soaked with water, either permanently or for part of the year.

facts.text: Wetlands sit between open water and dry land; their plants' roots are adapted to oxygen-poor, waterlogged soils.
They are among the most biologically diverse ecosystems, and their plants improve water quality by removing excess nitrates and phosphorus.
Wetlands exist on every continent except Antarctica, and their water may be fresh, brackish or salt.
Marshes are dominated by reeds, cattails and sedges, swamps by trees and shrubs; peatlands such as bogs and fens build up peat.
Hydrology, meaning how long and how often an area floods, is the most important factor that creates a wetland.
Wetlands provide services such as water purification, shoreline stabilization, storm protection and flood control.
The 2005 Millennium Ecosystem Assessment found wetlands more threatened by environmental degradation than any other ecosystem.
The largest wetlands include the Amazon basin, the West Siberian Plain, the Pantanal and the Sundarbans.

definition.text: Wetlands perform functions, such as storing water and cleaning it, that give people valuable benefits known as ecosystem services.

facts.text: The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment and the Ramsar Convention list services including flood control, groundwater recharge, storm protection, water purification, biodiversity, products, culture, recreation and climate regulation.
According to the Ramsar Convention, intact wetlands are often worth much more to society than the perceived gains from converting them to intensive land use.
Replacing wetland services would cost enormous sums for treatment plants, dams and levees, and many services cannot be replaced at all.
One analysis valued the storm protection wetlands provide against hurricanes at US$33,000/hectare/year.
Many wetlands are linked to groundwater and help refill aquifers, which supply much of the world's drinking water.
Coastal wetlands protect shores by reducing the speed and height of waves and floodwaters.
In highly developed areas, wetlands may be the only habitat left for pollinating insects, birds and mammals.

definition.text: Floodplains and other wetlands act as natural storage reservoirs that soak up excess water and so reduce flooding downstream.

facts.text: River floodplains let floodwater spread over a wide area, which lowers its depth and speed.
Headwater wetlands slow rain runoff and snowmelt so they do not rush straight into rivers, helping prevent sudden floods.
Wetlands hold extra water during heavy rain, reducing flood area, depth and duration.
Draining floodplains or hemming rivers in with levees forces the same rain through a narrower system, so flood peaks get higher and faster.

definition.text: Wetlands clean water by taking up nutrients and trapping sediment and the pollutants attached to it.

facts.text: Wetland plants slow the water so that sediment settles and is trapped, along with any heavy metals it carries.
This filtering is efficient, but each wetland has a threshold; too much fertilizer runoff or sewage causes eutrophication.
Heavy sediment from upstream deforestation can shrink wetlands and cause sharp biodiversity loss.

definition.text: Natural and specially built (constructed) wetlands can be used to treat sewage and other wastewater.

facts.text: Constructed wetlands use plants, soil and organisms to remove suspended solids, organic matter, nitrogen, phosphorus and pathogens.
The East Kolkata Wetlands in India cover 125 square kilometres and treat the city's sewage, whose nutrients feed fish farms and crops.
In cities, constructed wetlands also mitigate floods, store carbon and provide wildlife habitat.

definition.text: Wetlands naturally produce plants, fish and other goods that people harvest for their own use and for sale.

facts.text: Many fish spend all or part of their lives in wetlands; fish are the main protein source for about one billion people.
Rice, a wetland crop, supplies one fifth of all calories eaten worldwide.
Mangroves supply fuelwood, salt, fodder, traditional medicines, textile fibres, dyes and tannins.
The Lower Mekong basin's wetlands support over 55 million people.

definition.text: Wetlands are damaged or destroyed by drainage, pollution, dams, overfishing and other human activities as well as natural disturbances.

facts.text: Since 1900, 65–70% of the world's wetlands have been lost.
Wetlands are often drained with dykes and ditches to create farmland and increase economic output; some of the world's key farming areas were once wetlands.
Settlements built on drained wetlands become prone to land subsidence and rising flood risk.
Because wetlands hold water with little flow, they quickly concentrate toxic pollutants, harming native species.
Shrimp farming has wiped out large areas of mangrove, a damage hard to curb because of strong global demand.
In East Asia, up to 65% of coastal wetlands have been destroyed by coastal development.
Disturbances range from minor, through moderate ones a wetland recovers from alone, to severe ones needing human help.

verification.title: How much wetland has the world lost? Long-term and recent trends in global wetland area
verification.evidence: There has been a much (3.7 times) faster rate of wetland loss during the 20th and early 21st centuries, with a loss of 64–71% of wetlands since 1900 AD.

definition.text: Wetland conservation aims to protect wetlands and their natural functions from draining, flooding and other damaging change.

facts.text: Since the 1970s more attention has gone to preserving wetlands for their natural functions.
The Ramsar Convention, a treaty working since 1971, lists wetlands of international importance and promotes their wise use.
Ramsar methods include restricting access and teaching the public that wetlands are not wastelands.
Studies show wetlands can be conserved while improving the livelihoods of people who live in them, as with sustainably farmed dambos in Malawi and Zambia.
Wetlands cover at least six percent of Earth and became a conservation focus because of the ecosystem services they provide.
More than three billion people, around half the world's population, get their basic water needs from inland freshwater wetlands.
Coastal wetlands are estimated to save a median of US$447 billion in damages and 4,620 lives each year from storms.
Wetlands hold around 700 billion tons of carbon, mainly in peat soils, and sequester about 96 million tons a year.

definition.text: Wetland restoration helps a damaged wetland return to its natural path of development by assisting its natural processes.

facts.text: The level of restoration needed depends on how badly the wetland is disturbed; budget, time, goals and politics also shape the choice.
The cheapest, least intrusive level leaves the wetland to recover by natural succession once disturbance is stopped.
Partial reconstruction mixes natural regeneration with engineering such as ripping subsoil, mulching and mechanical seeding.
Complete reconstruction, the most expensive and intrusive, rebuilds the wetland from the ground up.
Traditional ecological knowledge offers a holistic approach that can raise wetland productivity, biodiversity and resilience.

definition.text: Wetlands can either store carbon and slow climate change or release greenhouse gases such as methane, depending on the wetland and how it is treated.

facts.text: Wetlands are the world's largest natural source of methane, emitting about 20–30% of atmospheric methane, on average 161 Tg a year.
Waterlogged, oxygen-poor soils favour methane-producing microbes.
Peatlands cover only 3% of land, but their degradation produces 7% of all CO2 emissions, as drained peat decomposes into carbon dioxide.
Salt marshes and mangroves sequester on average 210 g CO2 m−2 y−1, compared with about 20–30 g CO2 m−2 y−1 for peatlands.
Restoring coastal blue carbon wetlands to remove CO2 has questionable cost-effectiveness if judged only as climate mitigation.
Their flood control, groundwater and storm protection services help societies adapt to the worse floods and droughts of a warming climate.

definition.text: Valuing wetlands means mapping them, assessing the functions and services each provides, and using that information to rank or prioritize them.

facts.text: Over the longer term it needs wetland inventories and monitoring of a sample to track changes.
Rapid assessment methods score or rank a wetland's functions, services, species and health, usually from a single visit of less than a day.
Assessments help decide which wetlands to protect and how much compensation, such as restoring wetlands elsewhere, a loss requires.
Rapid methods are needed mainly when agencies face decision deadlines or have many wetlands to assess.
Satellite and aerial imagery, increasingly combined with LiDAR, map and monitor wetlands over large areas.

definition.text: An agroecosystem is a natural ecosystem that people have modified and manage to produce crops or livestock.

facts.text: Like other ecosystems it combines a physical environment, living organisms such as crops and wildlife, and the interactions linking them.
It is the basic unit of study in agroecology and regenerative agriculture.
An agroecosystem extends beyond the farm to the region its activity affects, through changes to species, energy flows and nutrient balance.
Intensively managed agroecosystems have simpler species, energy and nutrient flows than natural ones, and their excess nutrients cause eutrophication downstream.
More plant diversity in sustainable agroecosystems brings both ecological and economic benefits.
Forest gardens are probably the world's oldest and most resilient agroecosystem.
A report by the International Water Management Institute and UNEP suggested assigning value to ecosystems and recognizing trade-offs among users.
Agroecology tries to blur the line with natural ecosystems, for example through polyculture, wildlife buffer strips and organic farming.

definition.text: A coral reef is an underwater ecosystem built by reef-building corals, colonies of tiny animals called polyps held together by calcium carbonate.

facts.text: Sometimes called rainforests of the sea, shallow coral reefs are among Earth's most diverse ecosystems.
Reefs cover less than 0.1% of the ocean, about half the area of France, yet house at least 25% of all marine species.
Coral reefs are estimated to cover 284,300 km2, 91.9% of it in the Indo-Pacific region.
Most reefs grow best in warm, shallow, clear, sunny and agitated water, even though that water holds few nutrients.
Over 4,000 species of fish live on coral reefs.
Fringing reefs protect nearby mangroves and seagrass meadows from strong currents and waves.
Shallow tropical coral reefs have declined by 50% since 1950.
Coral reefs first appeared 485 million years ago, but most living reefs are less than 10,000 years old.

definition.text: Coral reefs are classed by shape and setting, classically as fringing reefs, barrier reefs and atolls, with platform reefs often added.

facts.text: A fringing reef is attached to the shore or separated from it by a narrow, shallow channel.
A barrier reef is separated from the shore by a deep channel or lagoon.
An atoll is a roughly circular reef surrounding a lagoon with no central island, usually grown from a fringing reef around a volcanic island.
Platform reefs grow wherever the seabed rises near enough to the surface for reef-building corals.

definition.text: Coral polyps cannot photosynthesize themselves but live in partnership with tiny algae, called zooxanthellae, inside their tissues.

facts.text: The algae feed the polyp with sugars such as glucose, glycerol and amino acids.
Stressed corals expel these colourful algae, a response called bleaching.

title: Coral reef ecosystem services

definition.text: Coral reefs give people valuable services, chiefly tourism, fisheries and protection of coastlines.

facts.text: About 500 million people benefit from coral reef ecosystem services.
The global economic value of coral reefs has been estimated at between US$29.8 billion and $375 billion per year.
Destroying one square kilometre of reef was estimated to cost between $137,000 and $1,200,000 over 25 years.
About six million tons of fish are taken from reefs each year; a well-managed reef yields on average 15 tons of seafood per square kilometre a year.
Southeast Asia's reef fisheries alone yield about $2.4 billion in seafood a year.
The World Resources Institute built tools to value reef tourism, shoreline protection and fisheries to support coastal policy.
A Belize study valued reef and mangrove services at $395–559 million a year; Bermuda's reefs were valued at $722 million a year on average.
