definition.text: Coral reefs protect coastlines by absorbing wave energy before it reaches the shore.

facts.text: Reefs can cut wave energy by 97%, helping prevent deaths and property damage; many small islands would not exist without them.
Reefs can damp waves as well as or better than artificial breakwaters, and restoring reefs is much cheaper than building breakwaters in the tropics.
About 197 million people living below 10 m elevation and within 50 km of a reef may get risk reduction from reefs.
Without the top meter of reefs, expected flood damage would double and costs from frequent storms would triple.
For 100-year storms, flood damage would rise by 91% to $US 272 billion without that top meter.

verification.title: The effectiveness of coral reefs for coastal hazard risk reduction and adaptation
verification.evidence: Meta-analyses reveal that coral reefs provide substantial protection against natural hazards by reducing wave energy by an average of 97%.

definition.text: Coral reefs are threatened by nutrient pollution, warming and acidifying oceans, overfishing and destructive land and sea uses.

facts.text: Coral reefs worldwide declined 14% from 2009 to 2018.
Local threats include coral mining, bottom trawling, blast fishing, overfishing and marine pollution, which persist where regulation is weak.
Greenhouse gas emissions warm the sea and raise sea level, causing widespread bleaching and loss of coral cover.
Ocean acidification slows coral calcification and speeds dissolution, though corals can partly adjust.
Overfishing and excess nutrients from land let algae outcompete and kill coral.
70–90% of today's warm-water coral reefs will disappear even if warming is kept to 1.5 °C.

title: Coral bleaching

definition.text: Coral bleaching is the stress response in which corals expel the colourful symbiotic algae living in their tissues.

facts.text: Rising sea temperatures from greenhouse gas emissions cause widespread bleaching.
El Niño events every 4–7 years bleach heat-sensitive reefs, with especially widespread bleaching in 1998 and 2010.
The Status of Coral Reefs of the World 2025 report found recovery time between warming events has shrunk from about a decade to five or six years in many regions.
Corals with some algal types (Clade A or D) resist heat bleaching better than those with Clade C, and some reefs become more resistant after a severe event.
Corals depend on single-celled algae (zooxanthellae) that live in their tissue and feed them through photosynthesis.
Most corals tolerate only a 4–5 °C range in temperature, and rising ocean temperatures may be the biggest threat to reefs.
One study of the Great Barrier Reef found 50% reef mortality after an extreme heatwave with a 3–4 °C rise.
Reefs can take decades to recover after bleaching.

notes: No crawled 'Coral bleaching' page; drafted from the Coral reef Threats section, which it shares with 'Threats to coral reefs'.

verification.title: Corals escape bleaching in regions that recently and historically experienced frequent thermal stress
verification.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences

title: Coral reef protection

definition.text: Coral reefs are protected mainly through marine protected areas and limits on fishing, pollution and coastal development.

facts.text: Marine protected areas aim at responsible fishery management and habitat protection, and can also serve restoration, biodiversity and economic goals.
Their effectiveness is still debated: some studied sites showed no difference from unprotected areas, and some caused local conflict.
Some protected areas provide local revenue roughly equal to what people would have earned without controls.
Protected areas seem able to protect reefs, but only with clear management and enough money.
Healthier Caribbean reefs have large parrotfish populations, found in countries that protect parrotfish and ban fish trapping and spearfishing.
Protecting networks of diverse, healthy reefs preserves the genetic diversity corals need to adapt to new climates.

contested_note: The sources say the effectiveness of marine protected areas for coral reefs is still debated.

definition.text: Coral farming, or coral gardening, grows coral fragments in nurseries and then replants them on damaged reefs.

facts.text: Gardening skips the early growth stages when young corals are most likely to die.
It relies on corals' natural ability to keep growing from fragments that anchor to new surfaces.
Coral nurseries became the most widespread and arguably most effective restoration method, largely replacing transplanting whole colonies.
Coral restoration grew because of unprecedented reef die-offs worldwide.

definition.text: A floodplain is the land beside a river, from its banks to the edges of the valley, that floods when the river runs high.

facts.text: Regular floods deposit nutrients, so floodplain soils are often very fertile.
Farms and cities have grown on floodplains to use their rich soil and fresh water, as in the Nile and Mississippi basins.
The risk of flooding has led to growing efforts to control floods.
Floodplains support diverse, productive and often very species-rich ecosystems.
Floodplain forests protect waterways from erosion and pollution and soften the impact of floodwaters.
Flood control, hydroelectric reservoirs and conversion to farmland are the main ways people destroy floodplain ecosystems.

definition.text: Most floodplains are built by rivers depositing sediment, both on the inside of their bends and when floods spill over the banks.

facts.text: A meandering river erodes the outside of each bend and deposits a point bar on the inside, building a level floodplain.
Water spilling over the banks lays down a thin layer of sediment, thickest and coarsest near the channel, forming natural levees.
In undisturbed rivers, overbank flow typically happens every one to two years.

definition.text: Floodplain ecology centres on the flood pulse: the yearly cycle of flooding and drying that brings nutrients and shapes life on the floodplain.

facts.text: Floods bring nutrient-rich debris and release nutrients from soil as it is flooded.
Many fish spawn as the flood begins, using the flooded river edge, and must grow fast before the water falls.
Floodplain plants and animals grow and die fast, letting them colonise shifting ground; floodplain trees are fast-growing.
Plant zones away from the river follow a gradient of soil moisture, oxygen and flood frequency.
Floodplain forests covered 1% of Europe in the 1800s and, less cleared than other forests, are important refuges for biodiversity.
Flood control sharpens the boundary between water and land, reducing habitat diversity.

definition.text: Floodplain flood control covers the rules, maps, insurance and works used to limit flood damage to people living on floodplains.

facts.text: River floods, especially on China's Yellow River, have been among the deadliest natural disasters, led by the 1931 China floods.
How far a floodplain floods depends on flood size, expressed as a return period such as the 100-year flood.
In the United States, the National Flood Insurance Program insures properties in flood-prone areas defined on flood risk maps.
Upstream development such as a large car park can raise flood levels, but the maps are rarely updated.
Some towns have been relocated off floodplains; elsewhere annual floods are part of the rural economy, supporting recessional agriculture.

definition.text: Floodplains can store phosphorus in their soils and plants, keeping it from overloading rivers downstream.

facts.text: Much of the phosphorus in freshwater comes from wastewater treatment plants and farm runoff, and too much is a problem.
Floodplain forests act as phosphorus sinks, and cutting rivers off from their floodplains worsens phosphorus overload.

title: Grassland

definition.text: A grassland is an area or ecosystem whose vegetation is dominated by grasses.

facts.text: Grasslands occur naturally on every continent except Antarctica and are among the largest biomes, covering 31–69% of Earth's land area.
They come as natural, semi-natural and agricultural grasslands.
One definition describes grasslands as kept open by fire, grazing, drought or freezing temperatures.
Grasslands support the greatest gatherings of large animals on Earth.
Their marketed and non-marketed ecosystem services are fundamental to the livelihoods of an estimated one billion people.
Grasslands hold about twenty percent of global soil carbon stocks.
They have been described as the most imperiled terrestrial biome, converted faster than forests yet given little protection.

distinct_from: Grassland management by fire and grazing

title: Types of grassland

definition.text: Grasslands are grouped into broad types by climate and setting: tropical, temperate, flooded, montane, tundra and desert grasslands.

facts.text: Tropical and subtropical grasslands and savannas get 90 to 150 centimeters of rain a year and support grazers like wildebeest and zebra.
Temperate grasslands include North American prairie, the Pampas and the European steppes, home to large herbivores such as bison.
Flooded grasslands such as the Everglades and Pantanal are flooded seasonally or all year.
During Pleistocene ice ages a cold, dry 'mammoth steppe' grassland covered much of the Northern Hemisphere.

distinct_from: Grassland management by fire and grazing

title: Semi-natural grassland

definition.text: A semi-natural grassland has wild, unsown plant communities but is kept open by human activities such as grazing and mowing.

facts.text: They can be extremely species-rich: a meadow in Estonia held a European record of 76 plant species in one square meter.
Almost 90% of Europe's semi-natural grasslands disappeared during the 20th century for political and economic reasons.
Agriculturally improved grasslands, fertilized and re-sown, are usually poor in wild plants.
Conservation groups buy these grasslands or pay landowners grants to manage them appropriately.

distinct_from: Grassland management by fire and grazing

title: Grassland carbon sequestration

definition.text: Grasslands store carbon mostly underground, in their deep roots and the soil, rather than in above-ground plants.

facts.text: Above-ground carbon does not last long because of grazing, fire and plants dying back.
Soil carbon makes up about 81% of all carbon in grassland ecosystems.
Carbon stocks are highest where rainfall is heaviest and fall as temperatures rise.
Soil disturbance, degradation, fire and erosion have caused large carbon losses, but good management can reverse them.
There is no agreement on how much carbon grasslands can store, partly because measurement methods differ and data are limited.

contested_note: Sources say there is no agreement on how much carbon grassland ecosystems can store.
distinct_from: Grassland management by fire and grazing

title: Grassland degradation

definition.text: Grassland degradation is the loss or decline of grasslands, driven mainly by farming, mining and other human land use.

facts.text: Global losses from grassland degradation are estimated at over $7 billion per year.
Of 70 grassland ecoregions, 21 are less than 20% intact and only 14 keep at least 60%; 47 have declined since 2000.
Most of the world's grasslands have been converted to fields of corn, wheat and other crops.
Grasslands are vulnerable because they are misclassified, poorly protected and cultivated.
Non-native grasses are expected to outperform native ones as climate change makes many grasslands warmer and drier.

distinct_from: Grassland management by fire and grazing

title: Afforestation of grasslands
article: Grassland#Afforestation or introduction of invasive species

definition.text: Planting trees on grasslands, often to store carbon, can damage grasslands and the services they provide.

facts.text: Forest-focused restoration risks misclassifying grassland as degraded forest, helping make grasslands the least protected biome.
A World Resources Institute and IUCN map of 2 billion hectares for forest restoration was criticised for including 900 million hectares of grasslands.
Grasslands and savannas benefit people too and are not supposed to be forests.

contested_note: Tree-planting campaigns are criticised for targeting grasslands and savannas where forests would not naturally grow.
distinct_from: Grassland management by fire and grazing

title: Grassland management by fire and grazing

definition.text: Many grasslands depend on disturbances such as fire and grazing to stay open, so how they are managed can make them persist or vanish.

facts.text: Grazing and fire keep woody plants from invading grasslands.
In Brazilian highland grasslands, areas without traditional burning every two years and cattle grazing could disappear within 30 years.
Protected areas that banned fire and grazing were quickly taken over by shrubs.

contested_note: The source says the dependence of grasslands on fire and grazing is still controversial.

verification.title: Preventing traditional management can cause grassland loss within 30 years in southern Brazil
verification.evidence: During the first 11 years without fire and cattle, woody encroachment in grasslands increased exponentially.
verification.note: 11 and 40 years are study intervals; findings on encroachment support the entry

title: Grassland restoration

definition.text: Grassland restoration aims to bring back degraded grasslands, though knowledge of the options is still limited.

facts.text: Only seven large, continuous grassland regions remain relatively intact on Earth.
Restoration costs vary widely and cost data are scarce.
Methods include prescribed fire, managing livestock and wild grazers, cutting trees and shrubs, controlling invasive species and reseeding native plants.
Success also needs policy recognition, standard indicators of degradation, research and data sharing.
The UN General Assembly proclaimed 2021–2030 the UN Decade on Restoration, led by UNEP and the FAO.

distinct_from: Grassland management by fire and grazing

definition.text: A peatland is a wetland whose soil is made of layers of peat, partly decayed plant material.

facts.text: Peat builds up because waterlogging cuts off oxygen, so dead plant litter only partly decomposes.
Peatlands cover around 3 million km2 and are the largest natural carbon store on land.
Peat soils store over 600 Gt of carbon, more than all other vegetation types including forests.
Natural peatlands reduce flood risk and erosion, purify water and regulate climate.
They are threatened by peat harvesting, drainage for farming (notably palm oil in the tropics) and fires.
Destroying peatlands releases stored greenhouse gases, worsening climate change.
Peatlands are most extensive at high northern latitudes.

definition.text: A mire is a peatland still forming peat; its two types are bogs, fed only by rain, and fens, fed by groundwater.

facts.text: Ecologists call any land with at least 30 cm of peat a peatland, even if it has been drained.
A bog sits higher than its surroundings and gets all its water from precipitation.
A fen lies on a slope, flat or hollow and gets most of its water from surrounding soil or groundwater.
Water passing through peat loses nutrients and becomes more acidic, so mires are usually nutrient-poor.

title: Peatland carbon storage

definition.text: Peatlands store huge amounts of carbon because plants keep adding dead matter faster than it can decompose in the waterlogged ground.

facts.text: Though only 3% of land, peatlands hold between 500 and 700 billion tonnes of carbon, over half the amount in the atmosphere.
Peatlands sequester 0.37 gigatons of CO2 a year.
Natural mires are a small CO2 sink but most emit methane and nitrous oxide.
The water table is the main control: when it drops, oxygen reaches the peat and decomposition releases more CO2.
Over millennia peatlands have had a net cooling effect on the atmosphere.

conflicts.text: Total northern peat carbon stocks are estimated at 1055 Gt C.
conflicts.note: Northern peatlands alone exceed the global total of 500-700 billion tonnes given in aab06bdb534a.

notes: Sentence 34ca5dac5e2b gives 1055 Gt C for northern peatlands alone, above the global 500-700 Gt (aab06bdb534a) and 'over 600 Gt' (76a49ee066cf); recorded as a conflict.

verification.title: Mismatch Between Global Importance of Peatlands and the Extent of Their Protection
verification.evidence: ABSTRACT Global peatlands store more carbon than all the world's forests biomass on just 3% of the planet's land surface.

definition.text: Peatlands are drained with ditches to lower the water table for farming and forestry, which turns them from carbon sinks into carbon sources.

facts.text: Agriculture and forestry, the main human uses, cover around a quarter of global peatland area.
Drainage lets oxygen into the peat, so it decomposes and releases carbon dioxide and methane.
Peatlands cover only 3% of land, but their degradation produces 7% of all CO2 emissions.
Degraded peatlands account for 5-10% of global carbon emissions from human activities.
Extreme drying can shift a mire into barren land with less biodiversity.

verification.title: Peatlands in the Earth’s 21st century climate system
verification.evidence: Anthropogenic disturbance, primarily agriculture and forestry drainage (10%–20% of global peatlands), results in net CO2 emissions, reduced CH4 emissions, and increased N2O emissions.

definition.text: In Southeast Asia, large areas of peatland forest have been drained and cleared for palm oil, trading economic gains against carbon, fire and biodiversity losses.

facts.text: Palm oil needs only 0.26 hectares of land to produce 1 ton of oil and has given income to smallholders in countries such as Indonesia and Malaysia.
About 12.9 Mha, or about 47% of Southeast Asian peatlands, had been deforested by 2006.
Emissions from palm oil on peatland are estimated at 12.4 to 76.6 t CO2/ha, and converted land can stay a carbon source after 12 years.
Drained peat dries into a flammable layer whose fires cause thousands of deaths each year.

verification.title: Current and future CO 2 emissions from drained peatlands in Southeast Asia
verification.evidence: Carbon dioxide (CO2) emission caused by decomposition of drained peatlands was between 355 Mt y−1 and 855 Mt y−1 in 2006 of which 82% came from Indonesia, largely Sumatra and Kalimantan.
verification.note: 12.9 Mha deforested by 2006 matches; 82% and 1.3-3.1% are other figures

definition.text: Drained and cleared tropical peatlands, especially in Southeast Asia, burn increasingly often, releasing huge amounts of carbon dioxide.

facts.text: Southeast Asian tropical peatlands cover only 0.2% of land but emit an estimated 2 Gt CO2 a year, equal to 7% of global fossil fuel emissions.
A severe fire can release up to 4,000 t of CO2/ha, and such fires usually burn for 1–3 months.
More than 2 million hectares burned in Southeast Asia in the past ten years.
Peat fires send smoke across international borders almost every year in Southeast Asia.

definition.text: Peatland restoration usually blocks drainage channels to rewet the peat and lets native vegetation recover.

facts.text: Rewetting cuts carbon release in the short term, and new plant growth eventually restarts peat formation.
The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report says conserving and restoring wetlands and peatlands has large economic potential to cut emissions, with benefits for adaptation and biodiversity.
The Convention on Biological Diversity names peatlands as key ecosystems to protect, and wetlands are also covered by the 1971 Ramsar Convention.
The Global Peatlands Initiative, formed in 2016, works to keep peatland carbon from being emitted.
Peatlands cover 400 million hectares, 3% of Earth's land surface.
They have been drained for peat extraction, farmland and forestry, damaging habitats, water flow, nutrient cycles and carbon balance.
Peatlands store carbon from dead plants, but drained and degraded peatlands release large amounts of greenhouse gases.
An intact peatland purifies water, filtering and storing metals and other toxins for long periods.

definition.text: The strip where land meets a river or stream, with its own water-loving vegetation.

facts.text: The name comes from the Latin ripa, meaning river bank; such strips are also called riparian buffer zones, corridors or strips.
Riparian zones act as natural biofilters, shielding waters from too much sediment, polluted runoff and erosion.
They give shelter and food to many aquatic animals, and their shade limits changes in stream temperature.
Buffer zones can cut nitrate pollution from manure and fertilizer washing off farm fields, and wetland riparian zones remove nitrate especially well.
Land beside a watercourse that stays waterlogged for a season or more is usually called a wetland instead, because of its hydric soils.
Because they support so many species, riparian zones are often protected under national biodiversity action plans.
Riparian zones may be natural, or engineered to stabilize soil or restore damaged land.

definition.text: The benefits riparian zones provide, from slowing floods and filtering runoff to wildlife habitat and recreation.

facts.text: River bends, plants and roots slow the water, which reduces soil erosion and flood damage, while trapped sediment leaves water clearer and builds banks.
They serve as wildlife corridors, letting aquatic and riparian organisms move along rivers instead of living in isolated groups.
Thinning riparian vegetation brings higher and more variable stream temperatures, and extreme temperature swings can kill fish.
Riparian zones raise nearby property values through views and amenity, and create space for fishing, swimming and boating.

definition.text: Leaving riparian strips undisturbed during timber harvesting so they keep protecting the stream.

facts.text: Undisturbed soil and vegetation along the stream give shade, leaf litter and wood, and hold back soil eroded from the logged area.
How well a buffer works depends on soil type, root structure, climate and plant cover.
Logging degrades riparian zones through added sediment, introduced or removed species and polluted water.

definition.text: Repairing damaged riverbanks through removing human structures, active rehabilitation, or simply giving them time.

facts.text: Clearing land and then flooding can quickly strip a riverbank of grasses and soil.
Methods range from erosion control and replanting to log sills, pin groynes and rock placement, invasive species control, and leaving areas alone to regrow.
Fast-growing pioneer 'weeds' can be used to kick-start succession, stabilizing soil until trees and grasses return.
Conservationists urge that the value of riparian ecosystem services be written into management plans, where it has usually been left out.

definition.text: An underwater ecosystem made up of seagrasses, flowering plants that grow in shallow coastal and estuary waters.

facts.text: Seagrass meadows rank among the most productive ecosystems on Earth, supporting marine life as diverse as coral reefs do.
Seagrasses descend from land plants that returned to the sea about 75 to 100 million years ago.
They grow on the continental shelves of every continent except Antarctica, down to depths of about 60 metres.
They prefer sheltered bays, lagoons and estuaries where waves are small and light and nutrients plentiful.
They shelter endangered species such as seahorses, turtles and dugongs, and are nurseries for shrimps, scallops and many commercial fish.
Pollution from land runoff, dredges and trawls, and overfishing are damaging meadows, which are being destroyed at about 3 square metres per second.

definition.text: The goods and services seagrass meadows give coastal areas, such as cleaner water, oxygen, food and shelter.

facts.text: Seagrasses improve water quality by locking up heavy metals and other toxins, removing excess nutrients and lowering acidity.
They release large amounts of oxygen into the water, and their roots oxygenate the sediment for the animals living in it.
Turtles, parrotfish, surgeonfish and sea urchins eat the grass, while small invertebrates feed on films on the leaves.
Conserving seagrass meadows supports 16 of the 17 UN Sustainable Development Goals.
Near small Indonesian islands without sewage treatment, harmful bacteria such as Enterococcus were 50 percent lower where seagrass was present.
Seagrass was once gathered as fertilizer for sandy soils and used to stuff mattresses.

definition.text: The carbon dioxide seagrass meadows pull from the air and bury in seabed sediment, part of coastal blue carbon.

facts.text: Seagrass meadows cover only 0.1% of the ocean floor yet account for 10–18% of all carbon buried in the ocean.
Per hectare they hold twice as much carbon dioxide as rain forests and can sequester about 27 million tons of CO2 a year.
Global seagrass meadows are estimated to store up to 19.9 Pg (billion tons) of organic carbon.
Carbon builds up in low-oxygen seabed sediments, where slow decomposition preserves it for decades to millennia.
Unlike land habitats that lose carbon to decay, fire or deforestation, marine sinks can keep carbon far longer.
Burial rates vary with species, sediment and depth, averaging about 140 g C m−2 yr−1.
Restored seagrass meadows began storing carbon in sediment within about four years.

conflicts.text: The Blue carbon article gives the average seagrass carbon burial rate as approximately 138 g C m−2 yr−1.
conflicts.note: Seagrass meadow gives about 140 g C m−2 yr−1 for the same average; likely a rounding of the same figure.

definition.text: How seagrass leaves and roots calm waves and hold sediment, protecting coasts from erosion and storm surge.

facts.text: Seagrasses are ecosystem engineers that reshape their surroundings physically and chemically.
Leaves slow currents so sediment settles and builds up the seafloor; without seagrass, currents carry it away and erode the bottom.
By reducing wave energy and building sediment they protect houses and cities from the sea and from sea-level rise.

definition.text: The role of seagrass meadows as sheltered nurseries for young fish and shellfish that later support fisheries.

facts.text: About half of global fisheries are estimated to get their start in seagrass habitats; lose the seagrass and the fisheries go too.
Seagrass gives nursery habitat to over 1/5th of the world's 25 largest fisheries, including walleye pollock, the most landed species.
A 2019 study found this role is poorly reflected in the decisions of the authorities who manage seagrass.
Gleaning for shellfish in intertidal seagrass feeds hundreds of millions of people, and small-scale seagrass fisheries act as a safety net for the poor.

definition.text: The worldwide loss of seagrass meadows, driven mostly by human activity.

facts.text: Some 30,000 km2 (12,000 sq mi) of seagrass has been lost in recent decades.
Loss sped up from 0.9% per year before 1940 to 7% per year in 1990.
Bottom-dragged fishing nets and boat propellers physically destroy meadows.
Excess nitrogen and phosphorus feed algae that smother seagrass and block light, starting a feedback loop that can replace seagrass with algae.
Overfishing top predators may boost algae indirectly through a trophic cascade that reduces small grazers.
Low-oxygen water starves seagrass roots and can kill meadows, and the decay of dead plants then uses up more oxygen.
Warming, sedimentation and coastal development also drive decline, and some models predict Posidonia oceanica will be extinct or nearly so by 2050.
Main protection tools are cutting nutrient and other pollution, marine protected areas, and transplanting.

definition.text: A disease of eelgrass, the most widespread seagrass, caused by the marine slime mold Labyrinthula zosterae.

facts.text: The pathogen enters leaf tissue, impairs photosynthesis and breaks down cells, leaving dark spots and streaks.
Warmer seas fuel outbreaks: after the 2015–2016 northeast Pacific heatwave, prevalence rose from 5–70% in 2013 to 60–90% by 2017.
Over the same period eelgrass shoot density fell by 60%.
Meadows with little disease can mark climate-resilient refuges worth prioritizing for protection and restoration.

definition.text: Re-establishing lost seagrass beds by transplanting plants or sowing seeds and other propagules.

facts.text: Communities in Virginia, Florida, Hawaii and the United Kingdom are restoring beds lost to human activity, and reintroductions improve ecosystem services.
Most restoration has used cuttings, rhizome fragments or cores taken from donor meadows; few projects use seeds.
Seed-based restoration has had low and variable results, with more than 90% of propagules failing to survive.
In Chesapeake Bay several million eelgrass seeds are gathered each year with a mechanical harvester.

definition.text: The release of greenhouse gases, chiefly methane and nitrous oxide, from wetland soils and plants.

facts.text: Wetlands are the world's largest natural source of atmospheric methane, which makes them a major climate concern.
They supply roughly 20–30% of atmospheric methane, about 161 Tg of methane a year on average.
Waterlogged soils run short of oxygen because microbes use it faster than it diffuses in, ideal conditions for methane-making microbes.
Warmer, more oxygen-starved soils rich in organic matter produce methane more efficiently.
Some wetlands also emit nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas with 300 times the warming potential of carbon dioxide.
Excess nutrients, mostly from human sources, sharply increase nitrous oxide release from wetland soils.
Wetlands can also act as greenhouse gas sinks; 14.5% of the world's soil carbon lies in wetlands, which cover 5.5% of land.

conflicts.text: The same section of Carbon sequestration also says 20–30% of the world's soil carbon is in wetlands, which make up 5–8% of land.
conflicts.note: Two different figures for the wetland share of world soil carbon (14.5% vs 20–30%) and of land area (5.5% vs 5–8%) on one page.

title: Wetland methane emission pathways
article: Greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands#Pathways of methane emission

definition.text: The three main routes by which wetland methane reaches the air: diffusion, transport through plant tissue, and bubbling (ebullition).

facts.text: Archaea produce methane by fermenting acetate, or by combining hydrogen with carbon dioxide.
When the water table is low, methane rising through soil passes a layer of methane-eating bacteria, which reduces emissions.
Plants with aerenchyma, porous air-carrying tissue, act as a shunt that lets methane skip that oxidizing layer.
In ebullition, methane pockets build in the soil until a bubble bursts, moving gas up too fast for microbes to consume it.

title: Controls on wetland methane flux
article: Greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands#Controlling factors

definition.text: The factors that set how much methane a wetland releases, such as water table, temperature, soil and plants.

facts.text: Net release depends mainly on how much methane made by methanogens escapes before methanotrophs oxidize it.
Emissions are measured with eddy covariance, gradient or chamber flux methods.
Big methane releases have been seen after droughts lowered the water table, since gas moves more easily through soil than water.
Plentiful cellulose and a soil pH of about 6.0 give optimum conditions for methane production.

title: Wetland drainage and greenhouse gases
article: Greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands#Human development of wetlands

definition.text: How draining wetlands for development, housing and farming changes their methane emissions.

facts.text: Draining lowers the water table, which lets soil bacteria consume more methane.
But drainage ditches stay waterlogged and warm, and can emit large amounts of methane.
Lowered far enough, the water table can turn a wetland from a methane source into a methane sink.

definition.text: An ecosystem in and around a body of water, as opposed to a land-based terrestrial ecosystem.

facts.text: It holds communities of aquatic organisms that depend on each other and on their surroundings.
The two main kinds are marine and freshwater ecosystems.
Freshwater ecosystems may be lentic (still water such as ponds and lakes), lotic (flowing water such as rivers) or wetlands.
Aquatic environments are relatively low in oxygen, so organisms must adapt, as wetland plants do by growing aerenchyma.
Algae, which build biomass from carbon dioxide using sunlight, may be the most important producers in water.
Algae and shallow-water plants together give estuaries and wetlands their extraordinary productivity, feeding fish, birds and amphibians.

definition.text: A salty-water aquatic ecosystem, the largest kind of aquatic ecosystem on Earth.

facts.text: Marine waters cover more than 70% of Earth's surface and hold more than 97% of its water and 90% of its habitable space.
Seawater averages a salinity of 35 parts per thousand, though it varies between ecosystems.
Marine ecosystems divide into zones by depth and shoreline, such as the open oceanic zone and the benthic zone on the seabed.
Seawater averages 35 parts per thousand salt, though salinity varies between marine ecosystems.
They range from coastal coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass meadows, kelp forests, estuaries, lagoons and salt marshes to the open ocean surface and the deep sea.
Pelagic systems regulate the global climate, feed the water cycle, maintain biodiversity, and provide food, energy, recreation and tourism.
Marine systems support billions of dollars' worth of fisheries, aquaculture, offshore oil and gas, and shipping.
Coastal capture fisheries from mangroves and coral reefs are estimated to be worth at least $34 billion per year.

definition.text: A marine ecosystem where the land meets the ocean.

facts.text: The world has about 620,000 kilometres (390,000 mi) of coastline.
Coastal habitats reach to the edge of the continental shelves, about 7 percent of the ocean's surface area.
They include many different habitats and are marked by high biodiversity and productivity.
Earth has about 620,000 kilometres of coastline, and coastal habitats occupy about 7 percent of the ocean's area.

definition.text: The community of organisms (neuston) that live at the ocean's surface, such as Sargassum seaweed and floating snails.

facts.text: Many ecologically and economically important fish species are neuston or depend on it.
The surface is on the front line of climate change and pollution.

definition.text: An aquatic ecosystem of low-salt waters such as lakes, ponds, rivers, streams, springs, bogs and wetlands.

facts.text: Freshwater habitats can be classified by temperature, light penetration, nutrients and vegetation.
Still-water (lentic) and flowing-water (lotic) systems are the two classic freshwater types.
Many freshwater organisms cannot tolerate salt, and irrigation water can pick up harmful levels of it.
They differ from marine ecosystems, whose water is much saltier.
The three basic types are lentic (still water such as ponds and lakes), lotic (flowing water such as rivers) and wetlands.
Freshwater ecosystems hold 41% of the world's known fish species.
Swamps, deltas and rivers make up 1% of Earth's surface, and land-based fresh waters produce about 1.5% of global net primary production.
Five broad threats are overexploitation, water pollution, changed water flows, habitat destruction and invasive species.

definition.text: A still-water (lentic) freshwater ecosystem of a lake or pond, with its living things and physical and chemical conditions.

facts.text: Lentic waters range from a temporary rainwater pool a few inches deep to Lake Baikal, 1642 m at its deepest.
Ponds have their whole bottom in light, while lakes have a dark deep zone, the profundal.
Ponds have an open-water pelagic zone and a benthic zone of bottom and shore.
Lakes are the main example of lentic (still-water) ecosystems, which also include ponds and wetlands, in contrast with flowing lotic waters.

definition.text: A flowing-water (lotic) ecosystem that drains the landscape, with its living things and physical and chemical conditions.

facts.text: Rivers are part of larger watersheds, where headwater streams feed ever larger channels.
Fast, turbulent water carries more dissolved oxygen and supports more species than slow pools.
Streams under forest canopy get most food from trees; wider, open streams get most from algae.
Threats include water loss, dams, chemical pollution and introduced species; dams cut spring floods and trap sediment, harming wetlands downstream.

definition.text: The environmental and human services aquatic ecosystems provide.

facts.text: They recycle nutrients, purify water, reduce floods, recharge groundwater and provide wildlife habitat.
Microorganisms, plankton, plants, invertebrates and fish help the water clean itself by breaking down organic matter and filtering water.
They support recreation and are very important to tourism, especially on coasts.
They also serve religious and educational uses, from pilgrimage to the Jordan River to ecological study of lakes.

definition.text: The non-living conditions that shape aquatic life, such as substrate, depth, nutrients, temperature, salinity and flow.

facts.text: Dissolved oxygen is often the key factor deciding how much and what kind of life a water body holds.
Nitrogen and phosphorus levels decide which algae dominate; too much algae can kill fish as it decays.
Decaying algal overgrowth in places like the Gulf of Mexico creates oxygen-starved dead zones.
Upstream dams can reduce spring floods and sediment, leading to saltwater intrusion in coastal wetlands.

definition.text: The stresses that degrade aquatic ecosystems once they exceed what the ecosystem can absorb.

facts.text: Stresses can be physical (temperature, flow, light), chemical (nutrients, oxygen-consuming materials, toxins) or biological (over-harvesting, exotic species).
Human-driven climate change disrupts where plants and animals live and has hurt deep-sea biodiversity, coastal fish and coral reefs.
Human-made waters such as ditches and aquaculture ponds trade biodiversity for their intended purpose.
The Great Lakes show how pollution, over-harvesting and invasive species can combine.

definition.text: A wetland that builds up peat, a deposit of dead plant matter, usually sphagnum moss.

facts.text: Bogs are one of the four main types of wetland; alkaline peat-forming mires are called fens instead.
They form where surface water is acidic and poor in nutrients, mostly in cooler northern climates.
Plants grow slowly, but decay is even slower in the oxygen-poor waterlogged soil, so peat piles up, sometimes many meters deep.
Most bogs get their water and nutrients from rain rather than ground or surface water, and have peat usually thicker than 30 centimetres.
The world's largest wetland is the peat bogs of the Western Siberian Lowlands, covering more than a million square kilometres.
Bogs host specialized species, such as carnivorous sundews and pitcher plants that get nutrients from insects.
Slowly accumulating plant material makes bogs a carbon sink.

definition.text: The classes of bog defined by landscape position, water source and nutrient supply, such as valley, raised, blanket and quaking bogs.

facts.text: Valley bogs form in gently sloping hollows and, because they rely on ground or surface water, occur only on acidic ground.
Raised bogs grow over centuries from a lake through marsh and fen until a rain-fed peat dome a few meters high forms.
Blanket bogs cover hilltops and slopes in cool places with rain on more than c. 235 days a year.
Quaking bogs are floating mats of moss and sedge, about half a meter thick, that move when walked on.

definition.text: Cutting peat from bogs to burn as fuel or to sell as a garden soil improver.

facts.text: Peat supplies more than 20% of home heat in Ireland and is burned for fuel in Finland, Scotland, Germany and Russia.
Russia is the leading exporter of fuel peat, at more than 90 million metric tons per year.
Because peat builds up so slowly, a bog is hard to restore once the peat is gone.
More than 90% of England's bogs have been damaged or destroyed, and in 2011 the UK announced plans to remove peat from gardening products.

definition.text: The benefits intact bogs give people, chiefly carbon storage and fresh water, along with food and recreation.

facts.text: If bog peat decays, its carbon escapes as carbon dioxide and adds to global warming; left undisturbed, bogs remain a carbon sink.
The peatlands of the former Soviet Union were calculated to remove 52 Tg of carbon per year from the atmosphere.
Rewetting drained peatlands may be among the most cost-effective ways to mitigate climate change.
Peat bogs store fresh water near the headwaters of large rivers; the Yangtze rises in the Ruoergai peatland.
Wild blueberries, cranberries, cloudberries and lingonberries are harvested from bogs, which are also used for ecotourism and hunting.

definition.text: The drying, drainage and warming that are degrading bogs, which take thousands of years to form and are very hard to recover.

facts.text: Northern European sphagnum bogs were often cleared and drained for farming, and European peatlands have dried quickly in recent centuries from drainage, peat cutting and burning.
Many Arctic and sub-Arctic bogs are warming at 0.6 °C per decade, twice the global average, and releasing large amounts of greenhouse gases.
These changes have caused severe declines in peatland biodiversity across Northern Europe.
Bogs are recognized as priority habitats by many agencies, including the UK Biodiversity Action Plan.

definition.text: A subarctic ecosystem of the Northern Hemisphere, roughly between 50° and 70°N, commonly called taiga.

facts.text: Boreal ecosystems span parts of North America, Europe and Asia.
Their plants range from black and white spruce to willows, wildflowers and alders, and caribou move in during winter to eat lichen.
They are less diverse than tropical systems but still hold a variety of species.
Wildfires, floods, mudslides and insect outbreaks drive secondary succession, which keeps the forest cycling.
Boreal soils hold about 338 Pg of carbon, comparable to the carbon in tropical ecosystems' biomass.
They are among the ecosystems most vulnerable to climate change.

definition.text: How warming changes boreal ecosystems and how their changes feed back on the climate.

facts.text: Thawing permafrost, milder winters and hotter summers displace cold-adapted species, increase forest fires and can turn boreal areas into other ecosystem types.
Plants and animals are already shifting northward, though plant migration may lag warming by decades to a century.
Permafrost thaw, fire and insect outbreaks have led some models to suggest boreal forests are now a net carbon source rather than a sink.
Permafrost stores double the carbon now in the atmosphere, which thawing can release as greenhouse gases.

definition.text: The services boreal ecosystems provide, led by timber and climate regulation through carbon cycling.

facts.text: Canada's boreal ecosystem is one of the world's largest carbon reservoirs and has high hydroelectric potential.
Boreal forests supply lumber and regulate water, soil and air quality.
Managing an ecosystem to maximize one service tends to reduce the supply of the others.

definition.text: The part of the ocean below about 200 m (660 ft), where light fades and the continental shelf gives way to the slope.

facts.text: It is cold, dark and under high pressure, and is the least explored biome on Earth.
Pressure rises about 1 atmosphere every 10 meters, reaching more than 1,000 atmospheres in places.
Without light there is no photosynthesis, so life depends on food sinking from above or on chemical energy at vents.
Its temperature is almost unchanging over long periods; no other habitat on Earth is so constant.
Salinity stays at about 35 parts per thousand throughout.
In 1960 the bathyscaphe Trieste reached the bottom of the Mariana Trench at 10,911 m, the deepest known spot in any ocean.
Deep-sea fish tend to be small, with slow metabolisms, and many use bioluminescence to hide their silhouettes.

definition.text: The depth bands of the deep ocean: the bathyal, abyssal and hadal zones.

facts.text: The bathyal zone, or continental slope, runs from 200 to 3,000 meters and mixes elements of the shelf and the abyss.
The abyssal zone lies between 3–6 km deep, and the hadal zone between 6–11 km.

definition.text: Deep-sea communities around hydrothermal vents that are powered by chemosynthetic bacteria rather than sunlight.

facts.text: They are among the few ecosystems on the planet that do not depend on sunlight for energy.
Tube worms such as Riftia live in partnership with chemosynthetic bacteria.
Water leaving 'black smoker' chimneys can reach 400 °C (752 °F), kept from boiling by high pressure.

definition.text: Lands defined by scarce water, where rainfall is balanced by evaporation and plant transpiration.

facts.text: The UN Environment Programme defines drylands as tropical and temperate areas with an aridity index below 0.65.
Drylands cover 41.3% of Earth's land surface, including 66% of Africa, 40% of Asia, 24% of Europe and 15% of Latin America.
They are home to more than 2 billion people, and 72% of drylands lie in developing countries.
Drylands include 45% of the world's agricultural land.
Their behaviour depends on many linked interactions among climate, soil and vegetation.
Unlike humid biomes, drylands redistribute water mainly through surface runoff.
They are highly vulnerable to climate change through shifting rainfall and land degradation.

definition.text: The four classes of dryland by aridity: dry sub-humid, semi-arid, arid and hyper-arid lands.

facts.text: Dry and sub-humid lands produce a large share of the world's crops and livestock.
By one rainfall-based measure, semi-arid lands get between 500 and 800mm a year.
Arid lands, with an aridity index of ~0.05-0.20 under the UNCCD, cover about 10% of the world's land and hold 20% of its people.
Hyper-arid lands cover ~8% of the world, get barely more than 100 mm of rain, and are excluded from the UNCCD's dryland definition.

definition.text: How climate change and human activity degrade drylands, bringing more drought, desertification and erosion.

facts.text: From 1982 to 2015, 12.6% of the world's drylands degraded due to human-caused climate change.
About 7.6% of global land has recently turned drier, an area larger than Canada.
Dryland degradation and desertification affect 213 million people, mostly in the Global South, and threaten food security.
Mobile pastoralism and other sustainable land management, restoration and climate-smart farming can soften these impacts.
Herders adapt by moving herds earlier, keeping smaller herds, changing water management and varying migration routes.

verification.title: Accelerated dryland expansion regulates future variability in dryland gross primary production
verification.evidence: Drylands cover 41% of Earth's surface and are the largest source of interannual variability in the global carbon sink.

verification.evidence: Despite an average global greening, anthropogenic climate change has degraded 12.6% (5.43 million km 2 ) of drylands, contributing to desertification and affecting 213 million people, 93% of who live in developing economies.

definition.text: The food, livelihoods, carbon storage and biodiversity that drylands provide to local people and the world.

facts.text: Millions of people in developing countries rely on dryland ecosystems for food security and well-being.
Dryland ways of life help halt climate change through carbon sequestration and conserve species.
Drylands provide significant global economic value through ecosystem services and biodiversity.
The Rio+20 conference in June 2012 stressed the intrinsic value of dryland biodiversity.

definition.text: Deliberate work to help degraded drylands recover, either by restoring their former function or by preventing further decline.

facts.text: Restoration is one of the three pillars of nature-based solutions as the IUCN defines them.
The IUCN and IPCC stress ecosystem restoration as a tool for climate mitigation and adaptation.
Dryland restoration is hard because rain is rare and variable, heat is high, soils are poor and invasive species spread.
Techniques target patchy vegetation: restoration islands, soil fauna, afforestation, exclosures, silvopastoralism and semicircular bunds.
The FAO offers 10 practice principles to guide ecosystem restoration.

definition.text: A restoration method that plants small, well-placed patches which then spread into the land around them.

facts.text: They suit patchy dryland vegetation and need fewer resources than large plantations.
Benefits include lower fire risk, less erosion, weed control, seed sources and wildlife habitat.
In drylands, patches spread more slowly than in humid ecosystems.

definition.text: Managing and restoring grazing lands so they keep producing while storing carbon and resisting desertification.

facts.text: Rangelands cover about 25% of drylands globally.
Rangeland restoration counts as a climate mitigation option because of its carbon sequestration potential, and it can improve herders' livelihoods.
Whether a practice is adopted depends heavily on local context, including ecological, economic, political and cultural factors.

title: Desertification narrative debate

definition.text: The dispute over whether the dominant story of spreading deserts, especially in the Sahel, is accurate.

facts.text: Desertification is a major threat to ecosystems and people, worst in Western Asia and South America.
Critics say the Sahel is wrongly seen as drying faster than elsewhere, a view rooted in colonial readings of land use.
The Sahel has in fact greened over recent decades.

contested_note: Some researchers reject the dominant desertification narrative for the Sahel, pointing to recent greening.

definition.text: Using local and indigenous knowledge and community involvement to protect and restore drylands.

facts.text: Case studies find that involving indigenous knowledge and local communities makes restoration more successful.
Silvopastoralism and agroforestry have been used successfully in dryland communities for centuries.
Indigenous fire practices can lower fuel loads and help prevent large, devastating fires.

definition.text: A partly enclosed coastal water body where river or stream freshwater mixes with seawater to form brackish water.

facts.text: Estuaries are ecotones, transition zones where river and sea environments overlap.
Tides, waves and salt water from the sea combine with river flow and sediment to shape them.
Mixing of fresh and salt water makes them nutrient-rich and among the most productive natural habitats in the world.
Most formed in the Holocene, when rising seas flooded valleys about 10,000–12,000 years ago.
Salinity ranges from near-zero at the river's tidal limit to 3.4% at the mouth and shifts with tides and seasons, making life hard.
Of the thirty-two largest cities in the early 1990s, twenty-two stood on estuaries.

definition.text: The benefits estuaries give people and nature, from fish nurseries and clean water to storm protection.

facts.text: Estuaries are nurseries for young fish and shellfish and sustain mangroves, seagrasses and salt marshes that support fisheries.
Commercial fisheries depend on estuaries for approximately 68 percent of their catch by value.
Estuary wetlands filter sediment, nutrients and pollutants from upland runoff, improving water quality.
Salt marsh grasses stabilize shorelines, buffering storms and sea-level rise and protecting infrastructure.
They are migration corridors for fish and habitat for migratory birds, supporting ecotourism.

definition.text: The classes of estuary by how they formed: drowned river valleys, bar-built, fjord-type and tectonic estuaries.

facts.text: Drowned river valleys, flooded as sea level rose, are the most common type in temperate climates.
Bar-built estuaries are shallow and cut off from the sea by sand spits or barrier islands, and are common in the tropics.
Fjord-type estuaries lie in deep valleys carved by glaciers.
Tectonic estuaries, formed by faulting, volcanoes or landslides, are few; San Francisco Bay is one.

definition.text: The classes of estuary by how fresh and salt water mix: salt wedge, partially mixed, well-mixed, inverse and intermittent.

facts.text: In a salt wedge estuary river flow dominates, so freshwater floats over a wedge of denser seawater.
Stronger tides cause partial mixing, and when tides dominate the water column becomes well mixed with no vertical salinity gradient.
Inverse estuaries occur in dry climates where evaporation far exceeds freshwater inflow.

definition.text: How pollution, overfishing, development, dams and diversions degrade estuaries.

facts.text: Estuaries gather pollutants from far upstream; long-lived toxins can bioaccumulate in aquatic life.
Fertilizer and waste runoff deplete oxygen and can create dead zones, cutting water quality and fish numbers.
Chesapeake Bay's oysters once filtered the whole estuary every three or four days; after overfishing it takes almost a year.
Dams and diversions shrank some great desert-river estuaries; the Colorado River Delta is now essentially a salt flat.

definition.text: Nutrient overloading of estuaries, mostly by nitrogen, that fuels algal blooms and harms plants, animals and fisheries.

facts.text: Feedbacks during eutrophication cut available silica and raise nitrogen and phosphorus, letting harmful algal blooms persist.
Blooms can briefly boost fish numbers, but continued oxygen loss then makes fish populations decline.
This can lower fishing sales; the US fishing industry employs 1.7 million people yearly.

title: Fen

definition.text: A fen is a peat-building wetland fed by mineral-rich groundwater or surface water.

facts.text: Fens are one of the main wetland types alongside marshes, swamps and bogs; bogs and fens together are called mires.
Their groundwater or surface-water supply gives fens more minerals and a more basic pH than bogs.
Fens store large amounts of carbon as peat, and destroying the peat layer can release it to the air.
Fens can clean nitrogen-rich farm runoff, releasing water with less nitrogen and fewer pollutants.
Conversion to farmland has been a major historical cause of fen loss, especially in Europe and North America.
Restoration often tries to bring back the site's water conditions, for example by blocking drains or ditches.

contested_note: Sources say it is controversial whether fens are net absorbers or emitters of greenhouse gases, because their waterlogged soils produce methane.

definition.text: The bog–rich-fen gradient arranges peatlands from species-poor bogs, through poor fens, to species-rich fens.

facts.text: Where a site falls on the gradient depends strongly on pH and on calcium and bicarbonate levels.
Rich fens get much of their water from mineral-rich sources, and their near-neutral water supports high biodiversity.
Poor fens are more acidic, with a pH of about 5.5 to 4, and their thicker peat cuts plants off from mineral soil below.

title: Freshwater biomonitoring

definition.text: Freshwater biomonitoring judges the health of a river or lake by surveying groups of organisms such as macroinvertebrates, plants and fish.

facts.text: Monitoring began because of health threats such as cholera from sewage, and moved from chemical tests to bacteria and then algae, fungi and protozoa.
Macroinvertebrates are often used because they are diverse, easy to collect and sensitive to many stressors; diatom algae are used for similar reasons.
A site's 'health' is often judged against reference sites with little human disturbance.

notes: No page of its own; drawn from Freshwater ecosystem lead and threats section. Consider merging into Freshwater ecosystem if no other page covers it.

definition.text: An intact forest landscape is a large, unbroken natural forest area with no sign of significant human activity or fragmentation.

facts.text: Technically it must cover at least 500 km2 (50,000 ha) and be at least 10 km wide, with minimal influence from economic activity.
Intact forest landscapes cover about 23 percent of forest ecosystems (13.1 million km2), almost all in tropical and subtropical forests (45 percent) and boreal forests (44 percent).
Only 10 percent of their global area is strictly protected, and about seven percent was lost after 2000.
Protecting them is often cheap, because the remoteness and low economic value that kept them undeveloped also lower protection costs.

definition.text: Lakes are commonly divided into a shallow shoreline (littoral) zone, an open sunlit water zone and a dark deep-water zone.

facts.text: Rooted wetland plants grow in the littoral zone near the shore.
In the open (photic) zone sunlight feeds algae; in the deep zone there is no sunlight and the food web runs on detritus from above.
The same zones are also called the pelagic, limnetic and profundal zones.

definition.text: In large lakes, summer warming splits the water into a warm upper layer and a cold lower layer that stay apart until autumn cooling mixes them again.

facts.text: The warm upper layer is the epilimnion, the cold bottom layer the hypolimnion, and the band of rapid temperature change between them the thermocline.
Water is densest at about 4 °C, which is why layers form as surface water warms.
Mixing to a uniform temperature is called lake turnover; in winter the layers form again in reverse beneath the ice.
Thermal stratification in larger lakes also affects how much oxygen each zone holds.

definition.text: Mangrove forests are productive wetlands of salt-tolerant trees growing in tropical and subtropical intertidal zones.

facts.text: About 80 mangrove species exist; they cannot survive freezing, which keeps them in warm climates.
Their stilt-like roots slow tidal water so sediment settles, forming a barrier that reduces coastal erosion from storm surge and waves.
The roots shelter many species and act as nurseries for young fish, including commercially important ones.
Mangroves are among the most productive ecosystems, with net primary productivity of about 208 Tg C per year, and generally act as net carbon sinks.
Mangroves sequester over 25 million tons of carbon each year, and losing them reduces carbon storage.
Where data exist, about 35% of mangroves have been destroyed, and around 2% of mangrove area has been lost each year since the 1980s.
Shrimp farming causes about a quarter of mangrove destruction; aquaculture, oil and timber production have also driven losses.
The world's largest mangrove forest is the Sundarbans, covering 10,000 km2 in the Ganges–Brahmaputra delta.

conflicts.text: Global mangrove carbon storage is estimated at 34 million metric tons per year.

definition.text: The outwelling hypothesis holds that carbon exported from mangroves as organic matter feeds detritus-based food webs in nearby coastal habitats.

facts.text: Mass-balance studies support it: mangroves usually fix far more carbon than they store, though the amount exported varies a lot between forests.
A mature mangrove forest reaches maximum biomass after about 20–30 years, so carbon fixed afterwards must be stored in sediment, exported or lost to the air.

definition.text: The intertidal zone is the shore area exposed to air at low tide and covered by seawater at high tide.

facts.text: It is divided into the spray zone and the high, middle and low intertidal zones, each with its own conditions and wildlife.
The high zone's changing conditions favour hardy animals such as barnacles, snails, mussels and hermit crabs.
The low zone is almost always under water, and life is more abundant there.

definition.text: Vegetated coastal ecosystems are plant-dominated shore habitats, chiefly seagrass beds, mangrove forests and tidal marshes.

facts.text: Together they cover about 50 million hectares and provide fish production, coastline protection, pollution buffering and high carbon sequestration.
They sit on organic-rich sediments, sometimes metres deep, whose carbon stocks can be several times those of forests.
When they are degraded or converted, the sediment carbon is exposed to oxygen and microbes release large amounts of greenhouse gases.
They are being lost to aquaculture, agriculture, dams, dredging, eutrophication, urban development and sea-level rise.

definition.text: Coral reefs, seagrasses and mangroves are linked systems that shield one another and exchange fish and invertebrates.

facts.text: Mangroves and seagrasses regulate the sediment, freshwater and nutrients that reach coral reefs.
Their ecosystem services reinforce each other: protecting fisheries in one raises fish biomass in the others, and tourism gains from both.

definition.text: A large marine ecosystem is an ocean region of roughly 200,000 km2 or more, defined by its seabed shape, water movement, productivity and linked food webs.

facts.text: The US agency NOAA developed the concept in 1984 to guide conservation and shared ecosystem-based management across national borders.
There are 66 large marine ecosystems, contributing an estimated $3 trillion a year and 90% of the world's annual marine fish catch.

definition.text: Mudflats, or tidal flats, are coastal wetlands formed in intertidal areas where tides or rivers have deposited sediment.

facts.text: A 2019 global analysis found tidal flats are as extensive as mangroves, covering at least 127,921 km2, with 44% in Asia.
They are key stopovers that let tens of millions of migratory shorebirds travel between breeding and non-breeding areas.
Once seen as economically unimportant, they were often dredged or converted to farmland; up to 16% of the world's tidal flats have disappeared since the mid-1980s.
Around the Yellow Sea, more than 65% of the mudflats present in the early 1950s had been destroyed by the late 2000s.

definition.text: An old-growth forest is a forest that has developed over a long time without disturbance.

facts.text: The FAO's related term, primary forest, means naturally regenerated native forest with no clearly visible human activity; one-third (34%) of the world's forests are primary.
Old-growth forests have large living and standing dead trees, layered canopies with gaps, and fallen woody debris on the floor.
After a severe disturbance it can take from a century to several millennia for a regrowing forest to regain old-growth character.
Their varied structure gives more diverse habitat than younger forests and shelters many rare and endangered species.
They provide services such as clean air and water, carbon storage, soil maintenance, pest control and climate regulation, which may matter more than their timber.
Carbon studies show old-growth forests store carbon more productively than younger forests.
As of January 2009 only 21% of Earth's original old-growth forests remained, and 90% of those in the contiguous United States in the 1600s have been cleared.
Primary forest was lost at 1.61 million ha a year in 2015–2025, less than half the 3.92 million ha a year of 2000–2015.

conflicts.text: Primary forests, which include old-growth forests, cover at least 1.18 billion ha (29%) of the total forest area.
conflicts.note: Lead gives 34% of the world's forests as primary (cited 2020); likely different assessment years.

definition.text: In forest dynamics, a stand passes through stand-replacing disturbance, stand initiation, stem exclusion and understory reinitiation before reaching old growth.

facts.text: In stem exclusion, trees compete for light; slow growers die and canopies close, so only very shade-tolerant plants survive beneath.
In understory reinitiation, scattered tree deaths open gaps that let shade-tolerant species establish below.
In old growth, more canopy trees die at different times, so understory trees grow at different stages and rates, giving a mixed-age stand.
A uniformly aged climax stand degrades fairly quickly into a new cycle of succession, so mixed-age stands are more stable.

title: Old growth in logging economics

definition.text: In logging terms, an old-growth stand is one past the economic optimum age for harvesting, usually 80 to 150 years depending on species.

facts.text: Old-growth forests were often logged first because they had the most valuable timber, were thought at risk of rot or pests, and occupied land wanted for faster-growing second growth.
Their large trees are economically valuable and have been aggressively logged worldwide, causing many conflicts between logging companies and environmental groups.
In some regions old growth is not the most profitable timber; coastal British Columbia is shifting harvests to younger second-growth stands.

definition.text: Peat swamp forests are tropical moist forests whose waterlogged soil stops dead leaves and wood from fully rotting, building a thick layer of acidic peat.

facts.text: They store far more carbon as soil organic matter than forests on mineral soil and are among the largest near-surface stores of land carbon.
Estimates of the carbon in tropical peat range from 50 Gt to 88 Gt.
About 62% of tropical peatland is in the Indomalayan realm, mostly Indonesia, and 36% is in Africa's central Congo Basin.
Drainage, logging and fires speed up decay of the peat and release its carbon as carbon dioxide.
Burning peat and vegetation in Indonesia in 1997 released up to 2.57 billion tons of carbon, equal to 40% of average yearly global fossil-fuel emissions.
Conserving and rehabilitating peatland earns more REDD+ emission reductions per unit area, at lower opportunity cost, than reducing other deforestation.

definition.text: The pelagic zone is the water column of the open ocean, away from the shore and the seabed.

facts.text: Down the water column pressure rises, temperature and light fall, and salinity, oxygen and nutrients change.
The pelagic ecosystem is based on phytoplankton, which need sunlight and so live in the upper sunlit layer.
Biodiversity drops sharply below the sunlit layer as oxygen, food and light dwindle and pressure and cold increase.
Pelagic fish are often migratory forage fish such as herring and anchovies, plus the larger predators such as tuna and sharks that follow them.
About 80% of ocean carbon fixation happens in the open ocean, which covers more than 90% of the ocean area.

definition.text: The open ocean is divided by depth into five layers: epipelagic, mesopelagic, bathypelagic, abyssopelagic and hadopelagic.

facts.text: The sunlit epipelagic zone is the only layer with enough light for photosynthesis; nearly all ocean primary production and about 90% of marine life is there.
The twilight mesopelagic zone gets only trace sunlight, and many of its animals use bioluminescence or rise to the surface at night to feed.
In the pitch-black bathypelagic zone most animals live on 'marine snow', detritus falling from above.
The hadal zone, below 6,000 m in trenches, reaches 10,935 m at Challenger Deep, with pressures of 1,100 atm.

title: River continuum concept

definition.text: The river continuum concept is a framework describing how temperate river ecosystems change in function from small headwaters to large rivers.

facts.text: It uses stream order to measure position along the gradient from small stream to large river.
Small shaded headwaters depend on leaf litter from land, mid-sized rivers get enough light for algae, and large rivers rely again mainly on outside inputs.
Animal communities track the energy supply: shredders thrive in small streams and grazers at mid-order sites.
Critics argue it rests on small temperate streams and cannot explain systems that switch between flowing and still states, which the flood pulse concept covers.

contested_note: Junk et al. argue the concept was built on small temperate streams and has been wrongly applied to all river systems.

title: Seagrass

definition.text: Seagrasses are the only flowering land-plant group that grows in the sea, usually forming meadows in shallow, sheltered coastal waters.

facts.text: About 60 fully marine species exist; they evolved from land plants that recolonised the ocean 70 to 100 million years ago.
Most species pollinate and complete their whole life cycle underwater.
Seagrass meadows hold more than 10% of the ocean's carbon storage and per hectare hold twice as much carbon dioxide as rainforests.
As ecosystem engineers, their roots stabilise sediment and their blades damp waves, reducing coastal erosion and storm surge.
They feed turtles, manatees and fish, and serve as nurseries for commercially valued fish, scallops and shrimp.
Although covering only 0.1–0.2% of the ocean surface, over 20% of global seagrass area has been lost since the late 19th century, at 1.5% a year.
About a quarter of seagrass species (15 of 72) could be rated Threatened or Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List.

notes: Species counts differ: ~60 (c5fbb3120188, 70e0518125f4) vs 72 (d7307584d990); probably different taxonomic scopes (e.g. Ruppia), so stated with their sources rather than as a conflict.

verification.title: Accelerating loss of seagrasses across the globe threatens coastal ecosystems
verification.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
verification.evidence: Our comprehensive global assessment of 215 studies found that seagrasses have been disappearing at a rate of 110 km(2) yr(-1) since 1980 and that 29% of the known areal extent has disappeared since seagrass areas were initially recorded in 1879.
verification.note: 29% lost since 1879 is consistent with 'over 20% since late 19th century'

title: Taiga

definition.text: The taiga, or boreal forest, is a biome of mostly pine, spruce and larch forest across the high northern latitudes, between the tundra and temperate forest.

facts.text: It covers 17 million km2, or 11.5% of Earth's land, with the largest areas in Russia and Canada.
Mean annual temperatures are generally −5 to 5 °C; summers last 1–3 months and freezing winters 5–7 months.
Taiga soils are young and nutrient-poor because the cold slows soil development.
The taiga stores more carbon than the world's temperate and tropical forests combined, much of it in wetlands and peat, and about twice as much per unit area as tropical forests.
Fire management costing about 12 dollars per tonne of carbon kept from release is very cheap compared with the social cost of carbon.
Its latitudes saw some of Earth's largest temperature increases in the last quarter of the twentieth century, with fewer extreme cold days helping tree-damaging insects.

notes: Source inconsistency: lead calls taiga the world's largest land biome (438e94f3c3b3), but Climate and geography says it is second in area only to deserts and xeric shrublands (a725e2f475ec).

definition.text: Fire is the main disturbance that renews boreal forest stands, and an area's fire regime describes the type, size and frequency of its fires.

facts.text: The boreal regime is dominated by intense crown fires or severe surface fires, often over 10,000 ha and sometimes over 400,000 ha.
Fire rotation is the average time for fires to burn an area equal to the whole ecosystem; individual sites may be skipped or burn more often.
In lichen woodland, large damaging fires recur roughly every 70 to 100 years.

definition.text: A temperate forest is a forest of the temperate zone, lying between the tropical and boreal regions.

facts.text: It is the second largest forest biome, with 25% of the world's forest area, behind the boreal forest's roughly 33%.
It spans latitudes of about 25 to 50 degrees in both hemispheres and includes deciduous, coniferous, mixed and rainforest types.
Lying where much of humanity lives, these forests were long cleared for cities and farming and suffer logging, mining, pollution and habitat loss.
Most temperate rainforests outside protected areas have been cut down.

definition.text: Tropical forests are forested regions with tropical climates, roughly between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.

facts.text: The tropical domain holds the largest share of the world's forests, 45 percent, ahead of boreal, temperate and subtropical forests.
Tropical forest ecosystems cover less than one-fifth of Earth's land yet hold about 50% of the world's species and about 60 percent of vascular plants.
They include evergreen rainforests but also open eucalyptus forest, tropical conifer forest, savanna woodland and mountain cloud forests.
No single scheme defines a forest, so estimates of tropical forest extent vary between sources.
Much current deforestation in biodiversity hotspots is driven by exports of beef, soy, coffee, cacao, palm oil and timber.
Valuing these forests' ecosystem services is widely held to encourage sustainable policy, but needs clear monitoring of outcomes.

verification.title: Tropical forests are home to over half of the world’s vertebrate species
verification.venue: Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment
verification.evidence: Using geographic range maps and data on species habitat associations, we determined that tropical forests harbor 62% of global terrestrial vertebrate species, more than twice the number found in any other terrestrial biome on Earth.
verification.note: 62% of terrestrial vertebrates, not 50% of all species

definition.text: A tropical rainforest is a dense, warm forest with high rainfall, typically within 10° north and south of the Equator.

facts.text: True rainforests have no dry season: every month averages at least 60 mm of rain, and mean monthly temperatures exceed 18 °C.
Heavy rain leaches nutrients, so soils are often poor; most nutrients sit near the surface because leaves and organisms decompose quickly.
Rainforests maintain biodiversity, store carbon, regulate the climate and support pollination; forests produce half of the Amazon's rainfall.
Tropical rainforests produce about 30% of Earth's fresh water and have among the highest primary production of land ecosystems.
Foods such as coffee, chocolate, bananas, mangoes and sugarcane originally came from tropical rainforests.
Mining, drilling and conversion to farmland drive deforestation; mineral and fossil-fuel extraction is often prioritised for economic growth.
REDD is a market incentive through which companies and governments offset emissions by financing rainforest conservation.

definition.text: Rainforests are organised into vertical layers, from forest floor and understory to canopy and emergent layer, each with its own community of plants and animals.

facts.text: The forest floor receives only 2% of the sunlight, so only low-light plants grow there.
The canopy forms a roof over the lower layers and contains most of the largest trees, typically 30–45 m tall.
Emergent trees rise above the canopy to 45–55 m, occasionally 70–80 m; only this layer is unique to tropical rainforests.

definition.text: Tundra is a biome where freezing temperatures and short growing seasons keep trees from growing.

facts.text: There are three types: Arctic, Alpine and Antarctic; vegetation is dwarf shrubs, sedges, grasses, mosses and lichens.
The boundary between tundra and forest is the tree line.
Arctic tundra is a polar desert with about 150–250 mm of precipitation a year and winter temperatures around −28 °C.
Biodiversity is low: about 1,700 vascular plant species and 48 land mammal species, though millions of birds migrate there each summer.
Its frozen soils store biomass as carbon, making tundra soil a carbon sink.
Arctic tundra is rich in petroleum, natural gas and uranium; the Yamalo-Nenets region produces 90% of Russia's natural gas.

definition.text: As warming thaws permafrost, stored carbon is released as greenhouse gases that cause more warming and more thaw, a positive feedback.

facts.text: The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report estimates permafrost emissions at 14–175 billion tonnes of CO2-equivalent per 1 °C of warming, against about 40 billion tonnes of human CO2 emissions in 2019.
A 2018 article suggested that at about 2 °C of warming, permafrost thaw would add a further 0.09 °C (range 0.04–0.16 °C) by 2100.
Thaw also threatens infrastructure built on permafrost, such as roads and pipelines.

definition.text: A forest is an ecosystem defined by a dense community of trees.

facts.text: There are hundreds of definitions; the FAO's is land over 0.5 hectares with trees taller than 5 metres and more than 10 percent canopy cover, not mainly farm or urban land.
The world has 4.14 billion hectares of forest, 32% of global land area or 0.50 ha per person, and 45% of it lies in the tropics.
Forests account for 75% of the biosphere's gross primary production and contain 80% of Earth's plant biomass.
Forests provide oxygen, carbon storage, climate and rainfall regulation, clean water, flood control, genetic reserves, timber, recreation, and subsistence for millions.
Forests can turn from a carbon sink into a carbon source if their plant diversity, density or area declines.
Most deforestation is now in the tropics, driven mainly by four commodities: wood, beef, soy and palm oil.
Global forest area fell by 178 million hectares between 1990 and 2020, about the size of Libya.
Some researchers note forests can also impose costs, such as reducing grazing and cropland or available water.

definition.text: The forest transition is the shift of a region from losing forest to gaining forested land overall.

facts.text: It happens through commercial tree plantations, agroforestry by small farmers, or natural regrowth on abandoned farmland.
It can be driven by the economic value of forests, their ecosystem services, or cultural change toward valuing forests for their own sake.
Net forest loss fell from 7.8 million hectares a year in the 1990s to 4.7 million hectares a year in 2010–2020, as new forests offset part of deforestation.
Large planting programmes in China, India, the United States and Vietnam contributed, and China banned logging from 1998 because of erosion and flooding.
New forests are not equivalent to old-growth forests in species diversity, resilience or carbon capture.
In 2025 about 813 million ha, around 20% of forest area, was in legally protected areas.
Countries move from high forest cover and low deforestation, through fast deforestation and low cover, to slowing loss, stabilization and recovery.
It is not a law of nature: population density, development stage, global markets and policy shape the pattern.
